 In The Supreme Court Of India
 Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction
 Criminal Appeal No(S). 3790-3791/2024
 Rakesh B Appellan
 Versus
 State Of Karnataka & Anr. Responde
 O R D E R

1. The appellant, who is the sole accused, was charged for the offences punishable under Sections 376 and 417 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, the IPC) and was acquitted by the Trial Court which has been reversed by the High Court vide the impugned order.
2. The case of the prosecution, in a nutshell, is that the prosecutrix and the appellant were in a relationship for a period of nearly 9 years from 2006-07 to 2015.

On the fateful day of the incident,
the appellant took the prosecutrix to a secluded house in a rubber plantation and thereafter,
committed rape on her.

The Trial Court, while disbelieving the evidence adduced by the prosecution,
found fault with the prosecutrix for the delay in registering her complaint with the police,
particularly, when she was an educated lady.

It also took note of the fact that the material witnesses,
namely, PW- 1 had turned hostile along with PW-7 and PW-8.
Accordingly, the evidence adduced by PW-13, who is the prosecutrix, was not accepted by the Trial Court.
3. On an appeal, the High Court was pleased to reverse the order of acquittal rendered by the Trial Court.

Thus, the appellant was convicted and sentenced to seven years for the offence punishable under Section 376 IPC and six months for the offence punishable under Section 417 IPC, with the sentences to run concurrently.
4. Learned Senior counsel appearing for the appellant submitted that the foundational facts are not in dispute.
Even as per the case of the prosecution, the educational qualification of the prosecutrix and the fact that the parties were in a relationship are not in dispute.
The Trial Court, while disbelieving the evidence adduced by the prosecution, was pleased to render an order of acquittal.
The High Court, though has power to re- appreciate the evidence, ought to have considered the reasoning adopted by the Trial Court while undertaking the said exercise.

In such view of the matter,
the order requires interference.

sentences.text: Learned Senior counsel appearing for the private respondent and learned counsel appearing for the State would submit that a very reasoned order has been passed by the High Court after re-appreciating the evidence.
Thus, there is nothing wrong in relying upon the evidence of the prosecutrix, who has to be placed on a pedestal higher that of an injured witness.
As there is no perversity, there is no need to interfere with the impugned order.
6. We find considerable force in the submissions made by the learned Senior counsel appearing for the appellant.
The parties were in a relationship for nearly a decade.
Material witnesses have turned hostile.
There is an inexplicable delay in lodging the FIR, though we are quite conscious of the settled position of law that, in a case involving Section 376 IPC, delay would not be material in all cases.

However, delay does make an impact if the surrounding facts would lead to an inference that the complaint was not given earlier, as the parties were still resolving the dispute between them which would not attract the penal provision.

7. The decision rendered by the Trial Court, which has got the benefit of seeing the demeanour of the witnesses is not expected to be reversed by an Appellate Court, unless an apparent perversity is found.
Though the view expressed by the High Court might be a plausible view, the same cannot be a ground to disturb the findings rendered by the Trial Court.
As stated, on the facts of the case, we do not find any perversity in the ultimate decision rendered by the Trial Court.
8. We also find that, even the offence under Section 417 IPC is not made out in the absence of any adequate material to support the same.
We only reiterate the fact that it was a courtship of nine years and thereafter, the relationship turned sour.

If the appellant wanted to sever the relationship,
he would have done it much earlier.
Therefore, even the finding rendered by the Trial Court in this regard is required to be confirmed.
9. In such view of the matter, the impugned order stands set aside and the appellant is acquitted of all charges.
Beil bonds stand discharged.

10. The appeals are allowed, accordingly.
11.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
